biggestGap: No pelvis: on all three figures the torso is one unbroken tube that ends in a straight skirt-hem at mid-thigh and the legs just hang from it. Both references break the body at the belt line — ribcage mass above, distinct glute/hip mass below — and that single break is what makes them read as bodies instead of mannequins in tunics.
notes: Human fighter vs Valheim player: reference wins. Ours reads naked — one flat skin tone from neck to toe with two floating pauldrons, and the side view is paper-thin through the chest with a pot-belly bulge in the silhouette panel. The Valheim player's clavicle-to-deltoid merge and belted waist give it a body; ours gives a wooden artist mannequin, though the face close-up (eyes, mustache, ink lines) is genuinely decent. Orc barbarian vs WoW grunt: reference wins decisively. Our orc is a trapezoid slab with a pinhead sunk straight into it — no neck, no trapezius ramp — legs half the width the torso promises, and the top panel shows the left arm fusing into the torso; the face close-up's droopy half-lidded eyes read sleepy, not menacing. The grunt's chest-to-pelvis-to-thigh chain carries its bulk; ours balances a fridge on two sticks. Dwarf fighter vs both references: closest call of the three but still a loss. Stocky ratios, beard mass, and the brown-plus-steel material breaks sell 'dwarf' at panel distance, and its silhouette panel is the only one with a readable waist; but the torso is still a straight barrel with no belt break, the hands are mitten lumps against the reference's separated fingers, and the huge glossy anime eyes fight the gritty proportions. Overall: reference wins 3-0. Poses and framing are fine (no harness bugs; all panels rendered), the faces have improved past creepy into passable, but the shared no-pelvis tube torso keeps every figure in mannequin territory.
